title: Will using AI automatically get you ostracized?

posts.author: Zetsuboy
posts.body:
Sup, everyone. Been with RPG Maker for years, but have yet to finish a first project. I've been putting a lot of time into one MZ project lately, and I really hope to finish it.
But I've always done this alone. And so, to make up for skills I don't have and the lack of money, I've had some resources in the game generated or edited with AI. Music, battler sprites, etc.
Some of the stuff I've manually edited myself. Some of the stuff I've collected from free resources too. Some came from old DLCs I had a long time ago.
But now I'm a bit apprehensive: when the time comes to post my first demo, which should be soon, should I be upfront about the use of AI? Will it make people hate me and not even give a chance to the content of the game? I had some thoughts, but all of them had obstacles.
A) Looking for people willing to help for free, in forums, reddit, etc.
BUT: How to even get them interested into the game without first launching a demo? Demo which contains AI material.
If the game gets a public, open a kickstarter to hire actual artists, musicians or even people to assist with actual development.
BUT: The initial AI hate might prevent me from even getting public in the first place.
C) I could just use placeholders from free resources?
BUT: That would require a lot of additional work to readapt everything built around the existing resources, as well as having to rework the entire game artistic direction, which I tried to keep somewhat consistent with the resources generated.
AND: The overuse of public resources might in itself also reduce public interest in the demo.
D) "Anything made by a human will always be better than AI slop"
BUT: Same as above. Would people even give it a chance if it looks bad?
I used to draw, but drawing is now a massive anxiety trigger, and then there's the music. The very core of my project requires A LOT of music and with specific vibes. But I can't make music and I am well aware learning pixel art takes way too long. I've tried in the past.
Thing is, I don't have time to do it all myself and still achieve a good quality. But I don't want this to be an excuse for my game to be sloppy and fail, and permanently ruin any kind of future I might or might not have in game dev.
I'm just looking to get this first demo out soon to get feedback and I'm worried about just how much placeholding will go into this alpha and how it would impact reception.
Please, I'm not looking for fights. I'm looking for talking, for guidance. If anyone has the time and will the actually chat with me in private, I can share more about my project and would really appreciate a more in-depth advice.
Thanks.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
Will using AI automatically get you ostracized?​
Click to expand...
Yes
Zetsuboy said:
should I be upfront about the use of AI?
Click to expand...
Yes
Zetsuboy said:
Will it make people hate me and not even give a chance to the content of the game?
Click to expand...
Yes
Let me answer those in more depth before tackling the other parts.
The fact of the matter is, yes. People's disdain for AI is strong right now that yes, there are going to be a group of people who do not want to support any person who is shown perpetuating the AI industry.
Lying about your AI usage - something a lot of AI users have started to do - is a bad idea because it's only going to trash your reputation even more once you do get caught, and trust me, people who are skilled in the industries that you generate (art, music, writing, etc) will notice something isn't right.
Zetsuboy said:
How to even get them interested into the game without first launching a demo?
Click to expand...
In the long, long distant past of just 4 years ago before everyone replaced their brain with AI, game developers used their archaic technique called "placeholders" and "grey boxing".
Placeholders can be literally anything. I personally use either some magenta circle or a big X to indicate a missing asset, but if you need more informative placeholders you can doodle a stickman, use stock photos, whatever else besides AI.
Grey boxing is using very simple (typically white or grey) environment assets to build the key parts of the level. At a later point, the level will be fleshed out with proper assets.
When trying to recruit people, you need to sell them on 2 things:
1) You are reliable and capable of finishing the game.
2) Your idea and why they should be interested. Use your words.
Zetsuboy said:
Would people even give it a chance if it looks bad?
Click to expand...
The reality is, probably not everyone. Nor would everyone want to try an AI slop game either. Don't target everyone.
You need to consider the optics of it though. Less people are going to throw a fit if you have crummy doodles you did then if you had AI art.
Zetsuboy said:
The very core of my project requires A LOT of music and with specific vibes. But I can't make music
Click to expand...
The truth is, there are a huge number of royalty free music libraries. And the nice thing about music is that it's not really formatted in specific ways to benefit specific engines. You can literally go to any royalty free music host and just buy a few of their tracks, convert it to ogg, and you're good to go.
Zetsuboy said:
I am well aware learning pixel art takes way too long
Click to expand...
Stop thinking about how many steps up the mountain you'll need to take and start taking the steps in front of you.
There are even professional, well respected indie games that have pixel art done by people who had never done pixel part prior to making their game. While professional pixel art can be very beautiful, the nice thing about pixel art is that it's very forgiving to even the amateurs. That's why pixel art has remained relevant to this day, despite having hardware more than capable of rendering realistic graphics.
Here's what I think:
Focus on getting the demo out - let that be the main focus "release the demo".
When you release it, be up front, but not preaching about your AI usage. Be honest about your usage, but don't sound defensive. State your usage truthfully and concisely:
"My game utilizes AI asset placeholders for music and art. The final release will not use these assets."
The fact of the matter is, people are adverse to AI, so you're going to have people turn away from it - some silently, some vocally. It can't be helped.
As a demo, the stakes are low. There
might
be reputational harm, but nothing you can't recover from by showing your commitment to doing things right.
My own game, when AI was first coming on the scene, used some AI assets. I became aware of what a parasite the AI industry is, and have long since replaced those assets. People can forgive.
In the future:
Making a game is going to cost -- time, money, or both. And you're going to have to be willing to make those sacrifices if you want it to be a commercial game people take seriously.
You can cut some corners as an indie dev. For example, stock assets. You can use places like ShutterStock, Story Blocks, Epidemic Sound, Zap Splat, etc. to access
human made
stock assets. Licenses can be a little bit expensive, but once you own them, they're yours to keep.
You could also pay musicians or illustrators to assist, but that is going to be far more expensive than buying stock asset licenses.
Where assets fail you, consider learning the necessary skills to a point of "good enough".
Get creative in other areas. A friend of mine, for his game's backgrounds, takes pictures with his phone and runs it through some filters to get a pretty creative effect. He's not much of an artist, but by thinking with the tools he has, he came up with something uniquely his own.
If you want to take your games development seriously, then you need to start taking investment into your game seriously.
Finally
You should really be aware of what you perpetuate by supporting the AI industry. That's a topic outside of the scope of this thread, but there are a lot of great articles and videos talking about how AI is leeching everything good from this world.
Just remember, creativity doesn't need to happen in a day.

posts.author: Maliki79
posts.body:
Generally speaking, you should announce and give credit to AI when used, just like you would for any asset.
Outside of that, bear the forum rules for using, requesting and sharing AI resources.
Lastly, I formally don't like using AI in general, but I have used it myself to help with things like action sequences and recently used it to offer suggestions on how to improve and correct my coding for plugins.  (Didn't help much in the long run either...)
Just be transparent in your use and don't ask us to help debug/fix/correct asset if you decide to lean all in on using AI.

Well, a lot of coherent music with a specific vibe is not going to be possible with AI, because whatever you make with AI is going to eventually start sounding repetitive and soulless. posts.author: ArtistocrArt
posts.body: Music is tricky but yeah if you can learn to make it yourself, that would be better in the long run. If you are planning on developing more than one game, then those skills will still be useful.

posts.author: Miggmaru
posts.body:
Anecdotally, I adore projects that are earnest but kind of bad, even outright hideous art and donky music. There's whole communities that love indie stuff like that. THIS community likes stuff like that, even. It's practically a rite of passage to make something really crusty. Some of the most beloved webcomics to me had me hooked with stuff that looked like and sometimes was made by a 15 y/o.
Since you're looking for guidance, my advice? Make something intentionally awful and stupid to shut down your brain's fretting, or least some other exercise to deal with it. It sounds like you're too afraid to fail, and this is something every artistic has to learn to cope with. In regards to your game, this sounds very ambitious as a first project. I recommend scaling it down, or writing a small project to make first so you're able to get the exp from finishing something. There's no way around this; AI won't fix your skill in putting together a game that large without finishing a more manageable project first.
I get the impression that you genuinely want to
create
, and not just generate things. Art is hard, and painful, but there's something indescribable in making something filled with yours and game partners meaning, with your own hands, that I don't think you'll find with AI. Good luck.

posts.author: rpgLord69
posts.body:
Of course you will probably succeed better if you use AI. And probably even better if you don't tell about it to anyone (but then you'll have to sit alone in your room crying and feeling shame, unless you're a psychopath). Though I think the majority wouldn't care about you using it.
The only reason (keeping the perspective away from macro-problems) for not using AI is if you want to "hobbify" what you're doing. If you like the idea of doing stuff with your own hands or human effort, want to pass time, want to actually learn or be proud of your own work, want to feel the joy of insights.
It also doesn't work if you're the kind of user who uses the first AI slop it generates, without properly prompting or refining for example images etc. I know I would be like that. Like half a year ago I tried what kind of images it could create, I asked it to create an rpg maker sprite sheet. It took like 5 mins for it to generate it (I was sitting on the computer really annoyed) and then the sprite wasn't even looking straight forward. Like seriously I wouldn't have patience for that.
Oh last point, I don't like the attitude of a lot of AI users, like "I don't have skills, money, time, motivation, effort etc, but of course I should be entitled to creating a game with custom battle systems, custom scenes, custom assets, custom everything". Nah, that's not how it works.

It depends on a few things.
What audience do you want?
There is a very loud group of people on the internet who despise the use of AI, for one reason or another. Some hate it more, some less. Then there is the people who either support AI or just don't care one way or another. Really it does not matter that much for the second question-
Do you understand the flaws and benefits of AI?
AI is a useful tool for many things, but it does depend on how you use it.
For coding, art, and music that you are wanting, always check the internet first, especially the rpg maker forums. You might very well find what you are looking for.
If what you are looking for is not present, then you can try to use AI
I find AI can be helpful for coding, as it can help you understand what terms do what. If it keeps failing, I suggest just turning to the forums and seeing what they can help cook up for you, otherwise learn coding the old fashion way and check the plugins or rpg maker script to see how you can achieve what you want, there are many rpg maker tutorials out there that can help with this.
AI art and music is likely not going to help you very much as it is very inconsistent and will likely not yield the results you want, i would stop if it keeps giving you unwanted results.
Do not solely rely on AI and always check its work, if generating something with AI is becoming frustrating, stop using it for that and try another method. AI is meant to make things simple, if it ends up being complicated, the AI is clearly not the tool for this job.
If you plan on using the AI permanently assets, expect backlash.
If you plan on using AI temporarily, backlash might still happen, but anyone who does help will be worth it.
If you plan on using no AI at all, no backlash and you are slightly more likely to get help, it just might not look as pretty.
My thoughts?:
- Use AI music and Art temporarily, as it may give people who decide to help an idea of what you want. You can also use it as a base for you to work on music and art yourself, if you so choose to.
- AI coding i see very little issue with using permanently, as its not something artistic, I would use it to help you learn how to code yourself, that way you will need it less and less as you use it (ironic, isn't it?), just remember to check everywhere else before you use this, as you will likely get better quality scripts or plugins than the AI can provide, you could also back track and edit the scripts the AI made in the past as your skills improve.
- Remember, AI is like a sword, you can use a sword to attack or defend, but not very well for surgery, remember when you need a sword and when you need a scalpel.
- Don't be too concerned with backlash, people who don't like AI use will either ignore you, convince you not to, or bully you. This happens to anything posted on the internet, so don't take what they say personally, as they are just some internet person in the end. Make the game however you want, just make sure you are aware of potential consequences.
- It will not ruin your reputation as a game dev, there are plenty of people who don't really care whether or not about the use of AI, as long as its good quality. You will get an audience, even if it may be smaller.
I hope you find what you need and hopefully my response was helpful.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
I will refrain from hyperbole and over dramatic, absolute statements.
If you just want to make a game for the fun of it, for yourself, or for your friends...do whatever you want that let's you enjoy the process and reach your goal.
If you want to release a game more broadly, then use whatever adds value to your game and you are satisfied with.
If you have a specific audience in mind, then you do have to cater to that audience if you want to be successful.
Not everyone hates AI. Some people are very vocal for or against AI. I think many people are ambivalent.
The forum has specific rules about posting AI content. And you should be upfront and transparent with however you used AI.
Will you be ostracized on the forum? Yes, by some, but definitely not by all.
I think if you are able to make a great game, then using AI as placeholders and being transparent about it could help you recruit others who are willing to work on the project with you, to replace the AI placeholders. But you need to have the game pretty much finished so you can showcase how good the game is to potentially entice others to help.
Also 100% reality. I think it is fair to say that the vast majority of users on this forum will never release a full, finished game for many, many different reasons. With that being said, using AI in a project that never gets finished wouldn't be a problem as long as you enjoy the journey. Until you are actually at a point where you can release a game, it is sort of a mute point.
Finally, hate is an incredibly powerful word. If anyone hates you simply for using AI, then those are people you really don't need in your life. At least in my opinion. There are so many worse things in the world than using AI for a small, hobby, indie developed game.  I just wish the people who are so vehemently and vocally opposed to AI would apply some of that same energy into those worse things.
But maybe they do and it just isn't apparent.

Click to expand...
Speaking from experience with this harsh reality, this likely comes down to poor planning.
I recommend pausing development - after you publish the demo - and building out documentation.
Mainly a game design doc and the core story script of the game.
When you are writing it out you can get a bird's eye view of the scope and decide how and where to scale back development.
Once you have documentation it's easier to stick rigidly to the plan instead of letting the design meander.
What is contained in the design doc is up to you. The more detailed the better, but obviously spending months or years documenting every minutia isn't very productive either.
My design doc currently contains descriptions of significant systems, sub systems, battle mechanics, stats and how they play into the game,  intended enemy AI, story goals and brief summaries.
It's also an evolving document. Things get revised or added as necessary.

posts.author: OmlyUltra
posts.body:
I'm not going to antagonize you here, since I can at least empathize with your stance, but I do think you're approaching this the wrong way.
I'm going to assume, from your post, that you are not making this game as your primary source of income. That being said, I don't believe I see a reason for you to use AI even if your target demographic was accepting of AI usage (which isn't hard to see that the general RPG Maker fan is not). Like some other posters have said, greyboxing and placeholder assets are good ways to make the experience playable without perfect implementation. You said that your game is very music-oriented, well, it is possible to greybox music too. By using AI, you're somewhat short-changing yourself on the experience of making a game, which I hope is the reason you're doing this in the first place.
The truth of the matter is that AI is becoming a prevalent aspect of many industries, and the games industry is no different. If you intend to make this project a portfolio piece to showcase your ability to use AI tools in development, so you can use it in an interview, etc, I can't say it's completely the wrong idea. But there are other engines out there that can get you better results with better integration anyway (Unity comes to mind). But it seems like you're making this game to, well, make something genuine, so be genuine about its implementation.
Final thoughts, I recall a report done recently that stated that the majority of (surveyed) video game players have negative emotions towards AI. I believe it was something north of 70%, so realize that should players notice that you have AI assets in your game, you're already slicing off 70% of a potential demographic that your game would otherwise appeal to. I'm not here to talk ethics with you, since it's more or less been covered extensively here, but I do believe you have avenues for your project that don't require AI. Would certainly help you learn more about game development as a whole.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
So, it’s far more nuanced that just lumping all gamers into one bucket and saying 70% plus are against AI.
In doing some simple research, you will see that there is actually a significant difference between the “core” gamer group and the “casual” gamer group. With core gamers being much more negative to AI and casual gamers being majority neutral.
And there are also generational differences in the perception of AI.
If you are really interested, there are studies and research on this specific topic for AI use in games and you can’t lump all gamers together.
Don’t trust statistics without sources that you can verify. Anyone with these concerns should do their own research and see how it compares to their specific use case for game development.

posts.author: Iron_Brew

Yes.
For anyone advocating against this stance: Ignore the facts, and look at public perception and reaction to GenAI.
I know it's hard, but: Ignore whether or not it's right or wrong. I used to be pretty hardline anti-AI and even though my stance has softened substantially, using generative AI is a poison pill right now.
It doesn't matter how good your game is, no amount of amazing mechnical design, considered narrative, or quality content can undo the reputational damage gen AI will do to the game. Look at Expedition 33, they won every game award, but the moment it turned out they used GenAI public perception has shifted irrevocably.
There is no undoing reputational harm, and right now the well is poisoned. Better to just spend the money or open microsoft paint and create something heartfelt over using GenAI.
Whether it's bad for the environment or theft no longer matters. The audience has decided that the issue is not nuanced, and as such if you are looking to create something for said audience, right now GenAI is suicidal.

I dunno man, generative AI does have implications generally (about the effort being put into the project at large), and I think that people saying that work using it is likely to be shonky at best have a point. At the same time, I think that getting defensive because other people dislike something you like isn't a particularly valuable use of time.
Like nobody's ever like "how dare you use AI tooling to identify that errant semicolon in your code", but when it comes to replacing entire swathes of human creativity? Yeah, I can see why people'd want to steer clear of that.
Even with my personal standards and inferrences put aside, the backlash faced by projects which choose to go ahead with those kinds of assets generally makes their inclusion feel short-sighted in the extreme. If you can choose to simply
not do a thing
to avoid backlash, why not just do that?
Sometimes pro-AI people feel almost bloody-minded in their pursuit of victim status. Nobody thinks you're cool or uncool for using AI, but the audience has been pretty clear in their preferences, and art is (I'd argue) - first and foremost - about the audience.
You wouldn't use paint made of baby tears, or a blood-diamond drillbit; even if they gave you decent results. And that's not necessarily because of ethics, it's because the audience simply won't buy a product made in a way that general consensus has deemed unethical - even if the creator doesn't give a damn.
